questions.q:
What is a "line of symmetry" in a paper-cutting activity?
[Recall]
questions.a: It is the specific line along which you fold the paper so that the two sides overlap perfectly. A wrong answer suggests the student thinks it is just any line drawn on a paper; this reveals they haven't grasped the concept of "overlapping" or "mirroring."

questions.q: The fold acts as a line of symmetry, reflecting the cut to the other half of the paper. A wrong answer (like "because the paper is thick") shows they are focusing on the physical material rather than the geometric property of reflection.
questions.a:
**Correct Answer:**
When you cut a shape from a folded piece of paper, you are cutting through two layers of paper at once. Because the paper is mirrored along the fold, unfolding it reveals the identical cut on both sides of the crease.

**Analysis of a Wrong Answer:**
A wrong answer (such as claiming the hole "magically doubles" or happens because the paper is "strong") reveals a **lack of understanding regarding symmetry and spatial reasoning.** It suggests the student is viewing the paper as a two-dimensional surface rather than a three-dimensional object with depth (layers) that is being manipulated through reflection.

questions.q:
Draw a rectangle on a grid. If you are given a vertical line of symmetry passing through the center, how do you find the position of a point that is 2 units to the right of the line?
[Apply]
questions.a: You place the corresponding point 2 units to the left of the line. A wrong answer (like "3 units" or "same side") reveals a failure to understand that reflection preserves distance from the axis.

questions.q:
Compare a square and a rectangle regarding their lines of symmetry. Which has more, and why?
[Analyze]
questions.a: A square has 4 lines of symmetry (vertical, horizontal, and two diagonals), while a rectangle has only 2 (vertical and horizontal). A wrong answer indicates they are not visualizing the diagonals of a square as valid folds that create overlapping halves.

questions.q:
If a student claims that any shape can be made symmetrical just by drawing a line through it, are they correct? Why?
[Evaluate]
questions.a: No, a line of symmetry must divide a figure into two identical halves that overlap perfectly when folded. If a shape is irregular, no line drawn through it will result in matching halves, meaning the student has confused "drawing a line" with "creating symmetry."

questions.q:
Design a simple 4-petal flower shape on a grid and explain how you would ensure it has rotational symmetry.
[Create]
questions.a: The flower should have 4 identical petals positioned at 90-degree intervals around a center point. A poor answer would show petals of different sizes or irregular spacing, indicating they do not understand that rotational symmetry requires identical elements spaced at equal angles.
